# Eval prompts

Five fixed prompts, one per main page shape. Each carries every fact the page needs, so a judge checks correctness against the prompt alone. Give the prompt to the agent exactly as written, with the skill loaded and no repository or web access. Save the page as `<id>.html` (and keep `<id>.src.html` when the skill writes one).

## arch: architecture and data flow

Draw how a photo upload works in our app. The phone asks the API for an upload URL; the API checks the user's quota in Postgres and returns a presigned S3 URL that is valid for 15 minutes. The phone uploads the original straight to S3, so the bytes never pass through the API. S3 sends an ObjectCreated event to an SQS queue. A pool of 4 thumbnail workers reads the queue, makes 3 sizes (256, 1024, and 2048 px wide), writes them back to S3, and marks the photo ready in Postgres. The CDN serves thumbnails from S3. Numbers from last week: the median original is 3.2 MB, the presign call takes 40 ms at p50, a thumbnail job takes 1.8 s at p50 and 6.5 s at p95, and the queue is empty 97% of the time. If a worker crashes, the message becomes visible again after a 60 s visibility timeout and another worker retries it, up to 3 times before it goes to a dead-letter queue.

## concept: a process over time

Explain how Raft elects a leader in a 5-node cluster. Every node starts as a follower. A follower that hears no heartbeat for its election timeout, a random value from 150 to 300 ms, becomes a candidate: it increments its term, votes for itself, and asks the others for votes. A node grants at most one vote per term, to the first candidate whose log is at least as up to date as its own. A candidate that gets votes from a majority, 3 of 5 including its own, becomes leader and sends heartbeats every 50 ms, which reset everyone's timeout. If two candidates split the votes and neither reaches 3, both time out and start a new election in the next term; the random timeouts make a second split unlikely. A node that sees a higher term in any message steps back to follower. Walk through one election: node C times out first at 162 ms in term 4, gets votes from A, D, and itself, and becomes leader of term 5 while B and E were still waiting.

## compare: options side by side

Compare three ways to run our nightly billing job, and recommend one. Option 1, cron on one VM: free beyond the VM we already pay for, but if the VM is down at 02:00 the run is skipped silently, and a crash halfway leaves some customers billed and some not. Option 2, a queue with workers: one message per customer, 3 retries with backoff, failed customers land in a dead-letter queue we can replay; it costs about $40 a month and a day of work to set up; a run of our 12,000 customers takes 9 minutes with 8 workers. Option 3, a managed workflow engine (Temporal Cloud): each customer is a workflow step with automatic retries and a full history we can inspect, and a crash resumes from the last finished step; it costs about $200 a month at our volume and a week to set up. Last quarter cron skipped 2 runs and one run crashed after 4,100 customers. The finance team needs every customer billed exactly once by 08:00.

## review: metrics and a weekly review

Make the weekly review page for the checkout service, week of 6 October. Error rate fell from 0.42% to 0.18% of requests after the payment-retry fix shipped on Tuesday. p95 latency fell from 840 ms to 610 ms; p50 stayed at 210 ms. Checkout conversion rose from 3.1% to 3.4%. There were 14 deploys and 1 rollback (Thursday, a bad config, reverted in 6 minutes). There were 2 incidents: a 23-minute card-processor outage on Monday that we could not prevent, and a 4-minute spike of timeouts on Friday from a slow database migration. The top three errors this week were card declined (61% of errors, expected), address validation timeout (24%, a new ticket is open), and cart expired (15%). One risk stays open: the address validation vendor has no retry, so its timeouts fail the checkout.

## bespoke: a figure no tag can draw

Explain why switching our primary keys from UUIDv4 to UUIDv7 made inserts faster. A UUIDv7 is 128 bits: a 48-bit Unix timestamp in milliseconds, a 4-bit version (0111), 12 random bits, a 2-bit variant (10), and 62 random bits. Because the timestamp comes first, new keys sort after old ones, so each insert lands on the rightmost leaf page of the B-tree index. UUIDv4 keys are random, so each insert lands on a random leaf page, which must be read into memory and often split. In our test of 10 million inserts into Postgres, UUIDv4 caused 4.1 million page splits and an index of 1.9 GB; UUIDv7 caused 60,000 page splits and an index of 1.3 GB, and the insert rate rose from 18,000 to 31,000 rows per second. The cost: a key reveals when its row was created, to the millisecond.
